title: Components of Health and Fitness
description: Definitions and sporting examples for all fitness components, distinguishing health-related from skill-related groups.
content_html:
What Is Health and Fitness?

Before looking at individual components, it helps to understand what we mean by the two terms. Health is a broad concept — it refers to complete physical, mental and social wellbeing, not just the absence of illness. Fitness, by contrast, is the ability to meet the demands of a specific sport or task. A person can be healthy without being particularly fit, and a very fit athlete can still have health concerns. In sport, coaches and sport scientists care about both — but fitness components are what they measure and train.

Health-Related vs Skill-Related Components

The components of fitness are divided into two groups. Health-related components underpin general physical wellbeing and are relevant to everyone, whether or not they play sport: aerobic endurance (cardiovascular endurance), muscular endurance, muscular strength, flexibility, and body composition. Skill-related components are performance-oriented — they are most important for sport and physical activity: speed, power, agility, balance, coordination, and reaction time. In the written exam you may need to classify a component into the correct group, so knowing both lists is essential.

Key Fact

Health-related components (5): aerobic endurance, muscular endurance, muscular strength, flexibility, body composition. Skill-related components (6): speed, power, agility, balance, coordination, reaction time.

Health-Related Components in Detail

Aerobic Endurance (Cardiovascular Endurance)

Aerobic endurance is the ability of the heart, lungs and circulatory system to supply oxygen to working muscles over a prolonged period of exercise. It is sometimes called cardiovascular endurance. It is essential for activities that last a long time at a moderate-to-high intensity — marathon running, long-distance cycling and rowing all demand high aerobic endurance. A footballer also needs aerobic endurance to maintain their performance level across a full 90-minute match.

Muscular Endurance

Muscular endurance is the ability of a muscle or muscle group to perform repeated contractions over a sustained period without becoming fatigued. It differs from muscular strength, which is about maximum force in a single effort. Sports that require muscular endurance include distance swimming, road cycling and cross-country running, where the same muscles must contract hundreds or thousands of times. A rower performing a 2,000-metre race needs high muscular endurance in the back, core and arm muscles to maintain stroke power throughout.

Muscular Strength

Muscular strength is the maximum force a muscle or muscle group can exert in a single contraction. It is important in sports that involve lifting, throwing, sprinting or explosive contact. A shot-putter needs very high muscular strength to generate force through the put. A weightlifter, a rugby forward clearing out a ruck or a gymnast holding a static position all depend heavily on muscular strength.

Flexibility

Flexibility is the range of movement possible at a joint. It is determined by the elasticity of the muscles, tendons and ligaments surrounding the joint. High flexibility reduces injury risk and can improve performance in sports where large ranges of movement are needed. Gymnastics and dance demand exceptional flexibility — a gymnast performing a full split or a diver entering a pike position both require high flexibility. Even team sport players benefit from good flexibility to avoid muscle strains and to move efficiently.

Body Composition

Body composition refers to the ratio of fat mass to lean mass (muscle, bone, organs and fluid) in the body. It is a health-related component because a high proportion of body fat is associated with increased risk of cardiovascular disease and reduced health, while a favourable body composition supports physical performance. Optimal body composition differs by sport — a heavyweight powerlifter may have a higher body mass with large muscle mass, while a distance runner is typically lean with a low body fat percentage to reduce the mass that must be carried over distance.

Skill-Related Components in Detail

Speed

Speed is the ability to move the whole body, or a body part, from one point to another in the shortest possible time. A sprinter needs exceptional whole-body speed over 100 metres. A cricket or baseball batter needs high arm speed to swing the bat effectively, while a defender in football must have speed to track runs from attackers. Speed is most obviously tested by sprint tests such as a 30-metre sprint.

Power

Power is a combination of strength and speed — it is the ability to apply maximum force at speed in a single explosive movement. A high jumper needs power in their take-off leg to propel them upwards; a tennis player needs power in their shoulder and arm to drive a serve; a sprinter's start reaction out of the blocks is powered by a powerful leg drive. Power is measured by the vertical jump test or the standing broad jump.

Agility

Agility is the ability to change body position or direction quickly and precisely while maintaining control and balance. It combines speed, coordination and balance, making it one of the most sport-specific attributes tested. A basketball player dribbling past defenders, a netball player evading a marker or a rugby player stepping around a tackle all demonstrate high agility. The Illinois agility test is the standard assessment used to measure it.

Key Fact

Agility is the ability to change direction quickly and with control — it is a skill-related component because it depends on coordination and balance as well as speed. It is most important in sports that involve frequent changes of direction, such as basketball, netball and rugby.

Balance

Balance is the ability to maintain the centre of mass over the base of support, either while stationary (static balance) or while moving (dynamic balance). A gymnast holding a handstand or a figure skater landing a jump must have excellent static and dynamic balance. A surfer maintaining their position on a board demonstrates dynamic balance. Balance is commonly assessed using the stork stand test, which measures the ability to balance on one leg for as long as possible.

Coordination

Coordination is the ability to use two or more body parts smoothly and efficiently at the same time in a controlled movement. Hand-eye coordination is crucial in racket sports, cricket batting and goalkeeping, where the hands must track and respond to a moving ball. Foot-eye coordination is essential for football and rugby. Coordination is measured by the alternate hand throw test, in which the performer throws and catches a ball alternately with each hand.

Reaction Time

Reaction time is the time taken from the moment a stimulus is detected (such as a starting gun, an opponent's movement or a ball being released) to the start of the response. A sprinter must react instantly to the starting pistol; a goalkeeper must react to a shot from close range; a badminton player must react to a fast smash. Faster reaction time can make the difference between reaching a ball or missing it. It is assessed using the ruler drop test.

Most team sports require a blend of several components. In football, aerobic endurance (90-minute match demands), speed (chasing the ball or outrunning defenders), agility (changing direction in tight spaces), coordination (controlling the ball) and reaction time (responding to a through ball) are all highly relevant. Muscular strength and power matter for heading, shooting and winning physical battles. The balance of components differs by position — a goalkeeper prioritises reaction time and power; a central midfielder prioritises aerobic endurance; a striker prioritises speed and agility. In the exam you may be asked to select and justify the most important component for a given position or sport, so always link your choice back to the demands of the role.

The demands of a sport determine which fitness components are most critical. A 100-metre sprinter needs maximal speed and power but relies far less on aerobic endurance because the race lasts under 11 seconds — the ATP-PC and anaerobic energy systems dominate. A distance swimmer needs high aerobic endurance and muscular endurance but does not need exceptional agility or reaction time. A gymnast requires elite flexibility, balance and coordination but is less dependent on cardiovascular endurance. Understanding this link between sport demands and fitness requirements is central to planning effective training programmes — a coach would waste time training a shot-putter for aerobic endurance when their event demands strength and power.
exam_tip_html: In the written exam you may be given a sporting scenario and asked to identify and justify the most important component of fitness for the performer. Always: (1) name the component precisely using the correct term (e.g. "aerobic endurance" rather than just "stamina"); (2) give a clear, specific definition; (3) link it directly to the demands of the sport — what does the performer actually have to do that requires this component? Avoid listing components without justification. If asked whether a component is health-related or skill-related, use the two classification groups and do not guess — memorise both lists.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Health-related components (aerobic endurance, muscular endurance, muscular strength, flexibility, body composition) underpin general physical wellbeing and are relevant to all activity levels.
  • Skill-related components (speed, power, agility, balance, coordination, reaction time) are most strongly linked to athletic performance and sport-specific skills.
  • Different sports prioritise different components depending on their physical demands — always link the component to a specific sporting example when answering exam questions.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a health-related component of fitness?
A) Agility
B) Reaction time
C) Muscular strength
D) Coordination
State two skill-related components of fitness.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: speed / power / agility / balance / coordination / reaction time. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by aerobic endurance and give one example of a sport where it is particularly important.
practice_questions.marks: A basic definition scores 1 mark (e.g. "the ability of the heart and lungs to supply oxygen to muscles during exercise"). A developed definition scores 2 marks (e.g. "the ability of the cardiovascular and respiratory systems to supply oxygen to working muscles over a sustained period, delaying fatigue"). A clear, relevant sporting example scores the third mark (e.g. "marathon running, where the performer must sustain effort for over 2 hours"). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by agility and explain why it is important for a basketball player.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): agility is the ability to change body position or direction quickly and accurately while maintaining balance and control (2 marks for a complete, precise description; 1 mark for a partial definition such as "changing direction quickly" without reference to control or balance).
Explanation of importance (up to 2 marks): for example, a basketball player must constantly change direction to evade defenders or close down opponents on the court — without high agility they would lose possession more easily and be unable to create scoring opportunities (2 marks for a developed, sport-specific explanation; 1 mark for a vague statement such as "it helps them move around the court"). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A hockey goalkeeper is preparing for an important cup final. Their coach has identified reaction time and power as the two most important components of fitness for their position.

Discuss how each component benefits the goalkeeper's performance during a match.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A developed discussion covering both components with clear sporting context. Reaction time: the goalkeeper must respond instantly to a shot or deflection from a short distance — faster reaction time means they can begin their movement before the ball has covered half the distance, making saves that would be impossible for a slower responder. Power: a goal kick or aerial clearance requires explosive leg and arm drive to send the ball the length of the pitch to relieve pressure; a goalkeeper with greater power can clear danger more efficiently. The answer identifies specific moments in a match where each component is decisive. Mastering answers may also note that both components interact — a fast reaction means little if the goalkeeper lacks the explosive power to reach the ball in time.
Secure (3-4 marks): Both components addressed with basic justification.
Developing (2 marks): One component addressed with limited justification.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: A 400-metre runner and a gymnastics floor performer both compete at a high level. Compare the components of fitness that are most important for each performer, and evaluate which performer needs a broader range of fitness components to succeed.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced comparison identifying key components for each. 400-metre runner: aerobic endurance (sustaining effort over ~45-50 seconds), muscular endurance (repeated stride cycle), speed (maintaining top velocity in the final 100 metres), reaction time (leaving the blocks quickly). Gymnastics floor: flexibility (splits, extensions), balance (holding static positions and landing from tumbles), coordination (linking complex movement sequences), power (propelling tumbles and leaps). Evaluation: gymnastics demands a wider range of components because the routine must demonstrate flexibility, balance, coordination, power and strength within a single performance; the 400-metre runner demands high levels of fewer components but at a more extreme level. Substantiated judgement with justification.
Secure (5-6 marks): At least two components for each performer with an attempt at evaluation.
Developing (3-4 marks): Components identified for both, limited comparison.
Emerging (1-2 marks): One or two relevant points with no comparison or evaluation. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following components of fitness is classified as health-related rather than skill-related?
Power is best defined as the combination of which two components of fitness?
The ability to maintain the centre of mass over the base of support while stationary or moving is the definition of _____.
The ability of the heart, lungs and circulatory system to supply oxygen to working muscles over a prolonged period is called _____ (also known as cardiovascular endurance).
Match each component of fitness to the correct sporting example.
right: A gymnast performing a full split on the floor exercise routine
A basketball player sidestepping rapidly to evade a defender
A sprinter responding instantly to the starting pistol

flashcard_questions.a: Cardiovascular system's ability to supply oxygen to muscles during sustained exercise.

flashcard_questions.q: What distinguishes muscular endurance from muscular strength?
flashcard_questions.a: Endurance sustains repeated contractions; strength produces maximum force once.

flashcard_questions.q: How is flexibility defined in sport science?
flashcard_questions.a: Range of movement at a joint, limited by muscle and tissue elasticity.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the five health-related components of fitness?
flashcard_questions.a: Aerobic endurance, muscular endurance, muscular strength, flexibility, and body composition.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the six skill-related components of fitness?
flashcard_questions.a: Speed, power, agility, balance, coordination, and reaction time.
Combining muscular strength and speed to produce a single explosive movement.
Changing direction quickly and accurately while maintaining balance and control.
The time from detecting a stimulus to beginning the physical response.

flashcard_questions.q: What is coordination in a sporting context?
flashcard_questions.a: Two or more body parts working smoothly together in a controlled movement.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is a marathon runner's most important component aerobic endurance?
flashcard_questions.a: The event lasts 2+ hours, demanding sustained oxygen delivery to muscles throughout.
Ratio of fat to lean tissue (muscle, bone, organs) in the body.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does a gymnast need high flexibility?
flashcard_questions.a: Gymnastics routines demand large joint ranges of movement throughout every skill.

glossary_terms.definition: A state of complete physical, mental and social wellbeing, not merely the absence of disease or injury.
The ability to meet the physical demands of a specific sport or physical activity effectively and without undue fatigue.
Components of fitness most closely linked to overall physical health and general wellbeing, including aerobic endurance, muscular endurance, muscular strength, flexibility, and body composition.
Components of fitness most strongly linked to athletic performance and sport-specific skills, including speed, power, agility, balance, coordination, and reaction time.
The ability to combine muscular strength and speed in a single explosive movement; sometimes expressed as the rate at which force is applied.
